chunks: Al-Hasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl narrated from Ẓarīf ibn Nāṣiḥ, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Ayyūb, who said: Al-Ḥusayn al-Rawwāsī narrated to me from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr al-Ṭabīb, who said:
I presented this narration to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, and he said: “Yes, it is true, and Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام used to instruct his officials accordingly.”

He said: He عليه السلام ruled that for every bone containing marrow there is a specified prescribed compensation when it is broken and then healed without deformity or defect. He made the prescribed diyyah six parts, and in wounds, the fetus, the eyelids, paralysis, limbs, and the thumb, he assigned six prescribed portions for each part. He made the diyyah of the fetus one hundred dinars, and he made the diyyah of a man’s semen until it becomes a fetus five stages: when it becomes a fetus before the soul enters it, it is one hundred dinars; for the nutfah, twenty dinars—namely when a man discharges away from his wife and casts his sperm while she does not want that, so Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام fixed for it twenty dinars, one-fifth; for the ʿalaqah, two-fifths of that, forty dinars; this also applies when a woman is struck or hit and casts it out; then for the muḍghah, sixty dinars if she miscarries it in such a case; then for the bone-stage, eighty dinars if the woman miscarries it; then for the fetus also, one hundred dinars if an enemy attacks them and the women miscarry in such a case. He imposed that upon the women from the side of the ʿāqilah likewise. If the child is born and cries—that is, crying—and they are attacked by night and the children are killed, then for them there is one thousand dinars for the male, and the female upon this reckoning is five hundred dinars. As for a woman who is killed while carrying a fully formed pregnancy and her child does not miscarry, and it is not known whether it is male or female, and it is not known whether it died after her or before her, then its compensation is in two halves: half the diyyah of a male and half the diyyah of a female, while the diyyah of the woman remains complete after that. He also ruled concerning a man’s semen when he discharges away from his wife and withdraws the fluid from her while she did not want that: half of one-fifth of one hundred from the diyyah of the fetus, namely ten dinars; and if he discharged into her, twenty dinars. He set retaliation for its injury and its indemnity in proportion to its diyyah, which is one hundred dinars, and he ruled regarding the diyyah of the fetus’s wounds according to the reckoning of the hundred, in accordance with what applies to the wounds of a man and woman in full.

He عليه السلام also ruled regarding the body and made it six prescribed categories: life, sight, hearing, speech, diminution of the voice through nasalization and hoarseness, and paralysis of the two hands and the two legs. He made this by analogy to that ruling, then with each of these things he established qasāmah according to the amount the diyyah reached. He made qasāmah in the case of life, for intentional killing, fifty men, and for mistake, twenty-five men, according to the diyyah reaching one thousand dinars. For injuries, qasāmah is by six persons, and whatever is less than that is reckoned upon six persons. Qasāmah applies in life, hearing, sight, intellect, voice affected by ghanan and baḥaḥ, and diminution of the hands and the legs. These are the six parts of the man. The diyyah for life is one thousand dinars; for the nose, one thousand dinars; for the whole voice lost through ghanan and baḥaḥ, one thousand dinars; for paralysis of the two hands, one thousand dinars; for total loss of hearing, one thousand dinars; for total loss of sight, one thousand dinars; for both legs together, one thousand dinars; for the two lips when completely removed, one thousand dinars; for the back when it becomes hunched, one thousand dinars; for the male organ, one thousand dinars; for the tongue when completely removed, one thousand dinars; and for the two testicles, one thousand dinars.

He عليه السلام set compensation for wounds in all the limbs—in the head, the face, and the rest of the body, regarding hearing, sight, voice, intellect, the two hands, and the two legs—in cases of cutting, breaking, cracking, crushing, exposing the bone, bleeding wounds, displacement of bones, and penetrating wounds occurring in any of that. Whatever bone is broken and healed without deformity or defect, with no bones displaced from it, its diyyah is known. If it exposes the bone and its bones are not displaced, then there are due both the diyyah of its break and the diyyah of its muḍiḥah. Every known bone that is broken has a fixed diyyah; the displacement of its bones is half the diyyah of its break, and the diyyah of its muḍiḥah is one-fourth of the diyyah of its break in what is covered by clothes, except the two forearm bones and the fingers. For an ulcer that does not heal, there is one-third of the diyyah of that bone in which it occurs.

If a man is injured in one of his eyes, it is measured by an egg tied over his injured eye, and it is observed how far the sight of his sound eye reaches. Then his sound eye is covered, and it is observed how far the sight of his injured eye reaches, and he is given his compensation according to that reckoning. Along with that there is qasāmah from the six divisions: qasāmah upon six persons according to the extent of what was lost from his eye. If it is one-sixth of his sight, the man swears alone and is given compensation. If it is one-third of his sight, he swears and another man swears with him. If it is half of his sight, he swears and two other men swear with him. If it is two-thirds of his sight, he swears and three men swear with him. If it is four-fifths of his sight, he swears and four men swear with him. If all his sight is lost, he swears and five men swear with him. That is regarding qasāmah in the eye.

He said: He عليه السلام ruled concerning one who had no one to swear with him and who was not trusted regarding what had gone from his sight, that the oath is multiplied against him. If it is one-sixth of his sight, he swears once; if one-third, he swears twice; if half, he swears three times; if two-thirds, he swears four times; if five-sixths, he swears five times; and if all his sight, he swears six times, then he is given compensation. If he refuses to swear, he is only given what he swore to and what was trusted from him as true. The wālī assists in that by questioning, observation, and verification in retaliation, legal punishments, and requital. If something affects his hearing, then similarly something is struck for him so that the limit of his hearing may be known, then that is measured, and qasāmah is according to the extent diminished from his hearing; and if all his hearing is gone, then it is upon the same basis. If immorality is feared from him, he is left until he becomes inattentive, then he is called out to; if he hears, they return the dispute to the judge, and the judge acts in it by his judgment and reduces some of what he had taken. If the deficiency is in the thigh or in the upper arm, it is measured with a thread: his sound leg or sound hand is measured, then the injured one is measured by it, so it becomes known what has diminished from his hand or leg. If the shin or forearm is injured, it is measured from the thigh or the upper arm, and the judge considers the extent of his thigh.

He عليه السلام ruled concerning the temple of a man: if it is injured and he cannot turn except by turning his whole body, then half the diyyah is due, five hundred dinars; whatever is less than that is according to its proportion. He ruled concerning the upper eyelid: if injured and split, its diyyah is one-third of the diyyah of the eye, one hundred and sixty-six and two-thirds dinars. If the lower eyelid is injured, its diyyah is half the diyyah of the eye, two hundred and fifty dinars. If the eyebrow is injured and all its hair goes, its diyyah is half the diyyah of the eye, two hundred and fifty dinars; whatever portion of it is injured is according to that reckoning. If the rawthah of the nose is cut off, its diyyah is five hundred dinars, half the full diyyah.

The compiler of this book, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The rawthah of the nose is the junction of its tip. If a penetrating wound is made in it that does not close, by an arrow or spear, its diyyah is three hundred and thirty-three and one-third dinars. If it is a penetrating wound that heals and closes, then its diyyah is one-fifth of the diyyah of the rawthah of the nose, namely one hundred dinars; whatever is injured is according to that reckoning. If the penetrating wound is in one nostril to the khayshūm, which is the barrier between the two nostrils, then its diyyah is one-tenth of the diyyah of the rawthah of the nose because it is half, and the barrier between the two nostrils is fifty dinars. If the shot penetrates one nostril and the septum to the other nostril, its diyyah is sixty-six and two-thirds dinars.
And the more common narration of our companions regarding that is the full diyyah.

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Prescribed blood money or financial compensation for killing or bodily injury.
key_terms.النُّطْفَةُ: The sperm-drop stage, treated here as an early stage with fixed compensation.
key_terms.الْجَنِينُ: The fetus, for which staged compensation is specified before and after development.
key_terms.الْقَسَامَةُ: A formal oath procedure used in proving certain injuries and homicide claims.
key_terms.الْمَعْقُلَةُ: The indemnifying kin-group responsible for payment in certain cases.
key_terms.الْمُوضِحَةُ: A wound that exposes the bone.
key_terms.نَقْلُ الْعِظَامِ: Displacement or moving of bones after injury.

ai.seo_question: What does this hadith say about diyyah for fetal injury, bodily wounds, and loss of limbs or senses in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith presents an extensive legal schedule of diyyah and injury compensation attributed to Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام and affirmed by Imām al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام. It covers fetal stages, bodily injuries, sensory loss, qasāmah, and proportional compensation across many limbs and wounds, making it a major jurisprudential text in the law of bodily injury and indemnity.
